abstract: Attribution to the Pockels effect of interfacial water, reported at interfaces between transparent electrodes and aqueous solutions, has relied on using an optical model to estimate the contribution of changes in the electrode's own carrier density to the electromodulation spectrum and subtracting this contribution. In this study, we test this attribution using the phase, without subtracting the electrode contribution with an optical model. Because the carrier response of the electrode follows charge modulation at several hundred hertz without delay, it has a common phase at all wavelengths apart from sign reversals of the response. However, the measured transmission modulation spectra at the interface between indium tin oxide (ITO) and 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ aqueous NaCl show a phase peak near 420 nm, where the ITO response becomes small. This peak cannot be explained solely by a step-like change due to sign reversal of the response. This peak appears even when the working-electrode potential, the modulation frequency, or the electrode is changed. Furthermore, this phase peak can be explained by a thin-film calculation assuming that a uniform refractive-index change on the electrolyte side contributes with a phase different from that of the electrode response. This result, an observation independent of the estimate of the electrode contribution, supports the attribution to the electro-optic effect of interfacial water.
